entries.title: Deportations Are Spiking. Judges Say Their Hands Are Being Forced.
entries.summary: Trump administration’s mass firings of immigration judges are influencing court outcomes, they say.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has created a climate of fear among the nation's immigration judges, firing those who don't go along with sweeping policy changes meant to boost deportations.

The Justice Department, which manages the nation's immigration court system, is relying on pressure campaigns to bend outcomes to match President Donald Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement vision, one current and three recently terminated judges told NOTUS.

They also said the department leadership has adopted new strategies to limit their discretion to rule in immigrants’ favor, which has effectively led to more deportations.

One current judge, who spoke on condition of anonymity over fear of reprisal, said colleagues were deciding cases with a new understanding that “following the law can risk their job if that law is inconsistent with current policy.”

“There's also a lot of fear among the immigration judges. The fact that following the law in a court is bravery is a little concerning,” the current judge said, before correcting themself. “That's a lot concerning.”

The Executive Office of Immigration Review, the Justice agency that houses the courts, has fired around 125 immigration judges since Trump took office. Nearly all of them received only an email with a couple sentences explaining that the president was asserting his authority under the Constitution.

The firings have continued in recent weeks. Additionally, around 100 additional judges have left with separation incentives or to retire, meaning more than one-in-four has left government.

While staff stressed they seek to implement the law in a neutral manner, the firings have effectively pushed judges to grant relief less often.

“For most of my colleagues, they’re going to do what they need to do to keep their job,” said Brea Burgie, a Colorado-based immigration judge who was fired in June.

“There is the constant stress of, ‘Is this the thing I'm going to do that gets me fired?’ When you’re living with that, the path of least resistance is, you don’t want to lose your job so you just comply,” Burgie said.

Some judges, who are also voluntarily leaving at unprecedented rates, have decided they cannot stay on the job in good conscience because they can't apply the law fairly.

“They're leaving because they feel like they can no longer execute due process,” the current judge said. “If you're a judge and you can't uphold due process in your court, or you feel like you can't effectuate that because policies are being made around you that don't allow you to to provide due process to people, that's a big concern for you because you feel like you are actually breaking the law.”

The second Trump administration has overhauled the deportation system to limit judges' latitude, former and current judges said, through new legal interpretations and policy memos that dictate how judges should run their courtrooms.

There are new requirements for faster decisions. The current judge noted they have little control over their schedule and anyone above them could be calling the shots on the movement of cases.

EOIR has packed as many as 150 cases for administrative actions on a judge’s docket some mornings, often with asylum seekers receiving little notice. If the migrants do not show up for the proceeding, judges must issue removal orders in absentia.

All of those factors appear to be bearing fruit for the Trump administration. After remaining relatively stable for much of Trump’s current term, according to the Transaction Records Access Clearinghouse, immigrant removal orders climbed this spring and spiked by 30% in June.

In some cases, threats to judges have been explicit.

In January, after a back-and-forth between Justice and federal courts over the legality of banning certain immigrants from being released from detention while awaiting court proceedings, Burgie received an email threatening discipline if she continued allowing bond hearings.

Burgie continued to do so, leaning on the federal court’s precedent. Days later, she was removed from cases involving detained immigrants. Months after that, she was fired. Like others, she was given no notice and had to leave immediately.

Eva Saltzman, a Chicago-based immigration judge, was in the middle of a hearing on July 30 when she received an email saying she was fired “effective immediately.”

“I read it again to make sure I understood it correctly,” Saltzman said. “I advised the parties we would be concluding immediately that we would not be able to complete that hearing that day.”

Saltzman then packed up her office and headed home.

She was the most senior judge on the bench in Chicago. She never let her guard down in the second Trump administration because she knew her location in a Democratic city and her low rate of deportation orders would put her on the Trump administration’s radar.

“As the agenda and the goals of the administration evolved and became more clear, I was concerned that doing my job in the way that I had always done would lead to me being terminated,” Saltzman said. “And I think that’s in part what happened here.”

Emmett Soper, a Virginia-based immigration judge who was fired last September, called that fear a “pretty effective technique” to achieve more deportations. Judges often have latitude in their decision making, he said, noting the same set of facts in many cases could allow a grant or denial to an immigrant’s request.

“If you have one of these cases where you are deciding whether to grant or deny, if you have this very real threat hanging over your head, it’s only human to be cognizant of that,” Soper said. “The judges are only human beings. They need to support themselves and their families.”

The Justice Department's moves have helped reduce the backlog of pending cases from its peak of 4 million to around 3.2 million.

A Justice spokesperson, when asked whether EOIR is targeting certain judges or seeking to influence court outcomes through personnel policy, said the department was looking to correct errors committed by its predecessors.

“After four years of the Biden administration forcing immigration courts to implement a de facto amnesty for hundreds of thousands of aliens, this Department of Justice is restoring integrity to our immigration system and encourages talented legal professionals to join in our mission to protect national security and public safety,” the spokesperson said.

The Justice Department is hiring new immigration judges to keep up with the departures. The department is advertising open positions as “deportation judges” and has eliminated some requirements for relevant experience

EOIR has onboarded 190 judges in fiscal year 2026, easily surpassing its previous hiring record for a fiscal year, including 118 since May. Nearly 90% of that more recent group were attorneys for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the military or prosecutorial offices. The department typically hired a large swath of its judges from immigration-focused private firms, but it has recently selected just a handful who had non-ICE immigration experience.

The current immigration judge noted the new hires are also receiving less training than they used to, which could mean cases that have been cleared might come back down after appeals because of rookie mistakes.

“They're all learning the immigration law and learning how to run their courts all at the same time,” the current judge said.
entries.author: Eric Katz

entries.title: Garbage Contaminating Camps In Gaza Renews Calls For U.S. Pressure On Israel
entries.summary: Lawmakers and the United Nations are warning of the spread of disease because of the unsanitary conditions in which most Palestinians are living.
entries.content:
The United Nations recently reported that most Palestinians in Gaza are living steps away from open sewage or human waste, and the strip is overflowing with garbage and rubble. Disease is spreading rapidly, and humanitarian groups and some lawmakers are redoubling demands for the U.S. to pressure Israel to ease overcrowding and stop blocking aid.

Dire conditions for those living in Gaza have persisted despite the 2025 agreement brokered by the Trump administration between Israel and the Palestinian militant group Hamas. An assessment cited by the U.N. in early April found that 60 percent of Gaza’s population was exposed to sewage or human waste within about 10 yards of their shelters, while more than 900,000 Palestinians were exposed to accumulated garbage in residential areas.

Data gathered July 19-25 by the World Health Organization suggested the two top health problems among Palestinians — acute respiratory infections and acute diarrhea — stemmed from poor conditions of water, sanitation and hygiene, also known by the acronym WASH. The U.N. also reported “significant” numbers of skin disease cases driven by clean water shortages. A U.N. WASH report earlier in July said 86 percent of households struggle to access a toilet or latrine, while 17 percent have observed open defecation. And the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem reported this summer “an extreme outbreak of rats and pests” in camps packed with displaced families, noting the link to garbage overflow, cesspits and rodent-borne disease.

“Sanitation is a chain, and all the chain has been devastated,” said Roba Daour Ziara, a Gaza-based public health officer at the charity Oxfam. She noted waste should normally move from toilets to treatment facilities, but Israeli attacks have destroyed hundreds of those facilities. The ones that remain need maintenance and power, rendered out of reach because Israeli authorities have sharply limited deliveries of repair materials, fuel, lubricant oil and generators, according to Oxfam and the U.N.

Earlier this month, 65 House Democrats — led by Reps. Andrea Salinas of Oregon and Kweisi Mfume of Maryland — wrote to President Donald Trump warning of “rodent and pest infestations throughout displacement camps … and insufficient rebuilding of the infrastructure needed for sewage, water and electricity.” The lawmakers blasted Israel’s restrictions on goods that it says have both civilian and military uses, as well as its limits on the normal operations of international aid groups. Tel Aviv’s approach “undermines a key component of the 20-point plan,” they wrote, referring to Trump’s stated roadmap for peace.

Even as Palestinians struggle, the Trump administration has said it will deliver stability and Israeli-Palestinian harmony through the president’s Board of Peace, most recently by announcing a plan for Hamas to disarm. Skeptics of the approach argue that the living conditions of Palestinians must be addressed to achieve meaningful progress toward regional peace.

“The President has a bold and ambitious plan to rebuild Gaza, which is well underway due to the efforts of the Board of Peace,” a State Department spokesperson told NOTUS via email. “US advocacy has enabled gains across key sectors: food assistance now reaches a majority of the population, health and nutrition services have expanded, and WASH support has scaled up, resulting in measurable improvements in food security, health outcomes, and access to safe water, along with temporary shelter support.”

Israel’s embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. Israeli officials have said they are facilitating appropriate deliveries.

“Israel remains committed to the coordination of humanitarian aid to ensure the appropriate medical, nutritional, and WASH response remains available to the Gazan civilian population,” Israel’s Coordination of Government Activities in the Territories unit said in a statement on X last week. The post listed Israeli approvals of shipments of generator spare parts by the U.N. and water containers by the Red Cross.

But Ziara noted that Oxfam and other aid organizations say Palestinians in Gaza still effectively face a “blockade,” and that improvements in humanitarian conditions are fragile and irregular.

Humanitarian groups, Ziara said, are seeking consistent engine oil flow to support daily services, not just specific operations; advocacy to shield WASH infrastructure from Israeli airstrikes; and more generators since Gaza remains without electricity — which means water treatment facilities share generators, limiting their output. She also noted that the growing section of Gaza controlled by Israeli forces includes many landfills. Without the ability to reach those sites, groups that collect solid waste, including the U.N. and Palestinian municipal workers, are instead using temporary dumping stations that are often located between Palestinian encampments.

Rachel Norris, the Gaza response director at the nonprofit Mercy Corps, said Gaza residents’ makeshift solutions fall short.

“Instead of large waste management trucks or any of the sort of facilities that would normally run, you are seeing donkeys pulling carts filled with waste,” she said, while some Palestinians have also built trenches or other temporary sites to contain waste. The result is latrines that Norris compared to “using a porta-potty that is not being changed out.”

A July 23 U.N. report found that 69% of the 181 displacement centers it assessed had visible sewage. At some sites, families were resorting to using slipshod toilets, buckets or plastic bags.

Meanwhile, amid shortages of clean water, Norris said, families face “impossible choices” about whether to use it for drinking, cooking, bathing or cleaning.

Addressing WASH is “foundational” and arguably even more important than increases in food supplies, according to Stacy Gilbert, a former State Department official who worked on global crises for over 20 years.

“You can keep feeding food into the situation, but if you’ve got poor sanitation it literally comes out the other end,” she said.

Gilbert resigned from her State Department role in 2024, citing the U.S. backing of Israel’s Gaza offensive. She described how some of the most vulnerable groups face outsize risks: When mothers are malnourished, they often supplement breast milk with formula, but even if that is available, it is dangerous to make with contaminated water.

Amid continued Israeli strikes and a deepening humanitarian crisis, Gilbert said the most dangerous part for Palestinians could be the lack of global attention to what’s happening on the ground, with garbage or debris left to rot and unexploded bombs littering the landscape.

“In many ways,” she said, “it's a more dangerous situation now because the world thinks the war is over.”
entries.author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed, Hamed Ahmadi
